Very low.
Okay, go ahead.
Sorry.
Yes.
I mean, it's a low.

Well, I think the cash at close isn't the issue.

I mean, there is other stuff.
Shall I just go through everything that we've highlighted?
Yeah.
So there's that, then there's the 400k, that is the, you know, the balance.
But you've got this five year payout with no interest and no security.
So as it stands, that doesn't feel very good at all.

I mean, they don't feel safe in the knowledge that they're going to get the rest of the money with, you know, over a five year period it's kind of negligible payout, but also with no interest and absolutely no security on it at all.
It does kind of feel like that is not something that they can rely on getting from you based on the way that it's worded.
So we just need some kind of guarantee on the cash.
It will have interest attached to it and over a short term it's usually some kind of base rate interest, but we can look at that.
Obviously it's attached to the valuation as well.
Then you've got a working capital ask of $700,000, which is, I mean, it's huge really, the way the deals are usually structured.
And obviously this is your offer, so you're entitled to offer whatever you want, but it is just as a cash and debt free situation.
And so I think the ask for the working capital needs to be.
I think it's just something that we need to discuss.
But currently where it is, it doesn't feel right, feels excessive compared to the actual payment that you're looking to put forward.
The way that I understand it, Dario, is that they have kind of almost like a subscription model for their business and so all of their clients are paying money into the business every single month.
And the way it works is like the newer clients pay in sort of like deposits and those definitely go towards work that hasn't been completed.
But they represent a very small portion of what they have as clients.

And the majority of their clients are just paying like a retainer or they're paying off the balance of whatever the project is over a period of time so that cash will continue to come in as they complete the jobs.
So for them to pony up 700k it feels excessive.
So that's another one.
And then we just, I mean there is a consultancy asked for the handover for one year, which I think is very reasonable actually.
There's nothing wrong with that in essence, but it's just that it kind of is very open ended at the moment.
I think they just want some reassurances around that there isn't an expectation for them to work full time in the business for a year.
And I'm pretty sure that that's not what you mean, it's more just that you require them to be available for the handover.
So if you could give us some clarity around that and then just on the non competes as well.
Because Ken has been working in marketing for like 150 years and for him to just like not ever work in the marketing industry again is, I mean is unlikely.
That's kind of the only place he really is likely to go if he was to get another job.
I mean he has no real intention of doing anything, but it's just he feels like he should be free to be able to get a job in the industry but certainly not set up another agency in the same space.
Competing for the same clients is cool.
So there's just like a, just a tweak on the language for that one.
And then the final one which is pretty major I think, is for you to have access to all of the staff for one to one interviews before the deal is closed, which represents a major risk.
And I'm sure you understand again, you.
Have access to what?
To their staff for one to one interviews before you've closed the deal with them is a huge risk for them.
I mean in the first instance there's no conversation being had with the staff that the company is for sale.
It's a huge risk.
If the staff find out that the company is for sale, many of them will feel worried and some potentially could start leaving the business if they felt that they were going to be sold on.
So what we need to do is figure out a way of sort of responding to that for you so that you obviously feel secure.

I would say that most of the representations and warranties in the SBA should cover anything that you would be concerned about so that you feel that you would need to speak to all of the staff one to one.
But again, I mean it'd be great if you could just kind of, you know, explain in more detail what's going on there.
So that's pretty much everything that we've got highlighted.
So happy to go through it again more slowly so you can give some responses.
Yeah, yeah.
So I understand the feedback.
Thank you for sharing.
I think the one aspect that is sticking the most is the valuation.
The business was possibly sized as a 4.3x multiple, but that was the next 4.3x multiple of last year.
Since then the business has declined.
I saw top line declining by maybe a 10% and I looked as much as possible in the P, L, the trailing twelve month P and L and even coming up with very conservative at back.
Excuse me, not Abex.
A very conservative replacement salary for Sharon and Ken.
That's pretty much the number.
I am coming with 515,000.
I'm sure that last year was greater than $515,000 adjusted EBITDA.
But I'm not making an offer based on what the business did last year.
Two years ago.
I am really looking at trailing twelve months.
Okay, so you can trail in twelve months.
Okay, well I will look at those numbers and get back to you.
But from their point of view, the valuation is low.
Particularly Dario, as I'm saying, we have another offer already that came in before yours at 3.5 million valuation.
So again, it's up to you how you want to take that information.
I do understand that.
I mean to be that is 6.8 multiple.
Unless there is additional addbacks in the trailing 12 months that I am not capturing, I don't think I'll be able to match that offer so transparently MD with a 6.8 multiple.
I have a lot of competing investment opportunities.
Again, if you guys tell me, hey, there are such and such advantage that you know that increase the overall bid that are $100,000 or $200,000.
I would like to look into that and see if I can come up with a higher offer.
But if there are no additional advects and I mean Ahmed and I had several conversations about it.
I listed pretty much what the the trailing 12 months PNL was showing.
If they're not back, coming up with a $3.5 million match will be very difficult.
You're looking at almost a 7x.
Well, I'm not saying that it needs to be a match.
Dario, they've really enjoyed the conversation with you and I think you're possibly the favorite.
But the situation is that lower offer than they've asked for combined with the working capital is kind of is Making it difficult based on you just being their favorite.
So what I would suggest.
Well, let us have a look at it.
But I think the main thing seems to be the conservative salaries.
So let's.
I do understand again in the first page of the loi, I have the breakdown of the addbacks that I understand from the business.
Now if there are other accounts where they have personal expenses that would bring up the overall ebitda, please let me know because that is what would make my.
Would make me change my mind in terms of the enterprise value.
Now if the archive would.
Enterprise value, but we can negotiate all the other points.
I think that's an avenue that would work with me as well.
Okay.

So the rest of the seller note currently is extended over five years with no security.

So.
More.

Yeah, but if you didn't make any follow up payments, basically you would be getting a discounted deal.
So what I usually see in these situations is that the sellers have like a lien on the company so that if you don't make any further payments that they have a right to claim the company back.
Yeah, I think we're saying the same thing.
I think I would be okay with an approach similar to what you are discussing.
Okay, cool.
All right, that would be great then.
Derek.

So Sharon will show you the accounts that do need working capital and the ones that are being paid every single month.

Right.

Yeah.

Yeah, I mean, the idea is that they hand the business over, not that they work in it.
So that sounds like we're agreeing.

But again if, I mean maybe this is just something that you can assure Ken and Ken can assure you somewhat as well that he has no intention of competing with you.

Okay.

summary.action_items:
**Andrew Day**
Review and clarify the trailing 12-month numbers that Dario used in his valuation calculations (26:10)
Obtain detailed account breakdown from Sharon showing which client accounts need working capital support versus monthly retainer payments (17:04)
Investigate the down months in P&L and get clarity on payment timing/accounting issues (18:27)
Identify any additional addbacks or personal expenses that could increase EBITDA calculation (27:10)

**Dario**
Consider slight improvement to overall offer if additional addbacks are identified (27:10)
Propose middle-ground solution for working capital requirement negotiations (18:27)
Develop better transition consulting plan during due diligence phase focusing on successful transfer rather than time commitment (19:30)

**Sharon**
Provide detailed client account analysis showing deposit-based vs. retainer-based payment structures (17:04)
Explain rationale behind negative months in trailing 12-month P&L (18:27)
summary.overview:
- Dario's current offer is $3.5M, but they face valuation challenges due to different EBITDA calculation methods and expected upcoming offers.
- Seller financing includes a $400K balance with unrealistic terms of a 5-year payout without interest, raising concerns about its viability.
- The working capital requirement of $700K is viewed as excessive, complicating the cash-and-debt-free aspect of the transaction.
- Transition consulting requests involve a one-year handover period, but clarity on the time commitment remains unresolved.
- Proposed modifications to the non-compete clause are necessary to support Ken's future employment prospects post-sale.
- Potential risks arise from the staff interview requirements, which could lead to employee departures once the sale is publicly known.
- Dario is open to utilizing the business as collateral for seller note payments, offering a lien structure for added security.
- Competitive analysis indicates a rival offer using a 6.8x multiple, contrasting with Dario's lower valuation approach and highlighting market pressures.
- Salary replacement expectations show significant divergence, affecting negotiations around compensation structures.
- Identified addback opportunities suggest that including personal expenses could enhance overall valuation, warranting further examination.
summary.short_summary: Dario's current offer stands at $3.5M, facing valuation challenges primarily due to differing EBITDA calculation methods and anticipated competitive offers. Seller financing poses issues with a $400K balance that has unrealistic terms, raising concerns about its viability. Additionally, the working capital requirement of $700K complicates the cash-and-debt-free structure of the transaction. Transition consulting requests suggest a one-year handover, but the commitment level remains unclear. Modifications to the non-compete clause are proposed to enhance Ken's post-sale employment prospects. The potential risks from staff interviews could lead to employee departures post-sale announcement. Dario is open to using business collateral for seller note payments, and competitive analysis shows a rival offer using a 6.8x multiple, emphasizing market pressures. Diverging salary replacement expectations and identified addback opportunities for personal expenses could also enhance valuation.
